Q3130: Capital of New South Wales and Australia's largest city, around Sydney Harbour.
Founded in 1788 as a British penal colony, the first European settlement in Australia.
The Sydney Opera House (a World Heritage Site) and Harbour Bridge are its icons; Bondi Beach is in the east.
Hosted the 2000 Summer Olympics; it is not Australia's capital (that is Canberra).
Q35381: Sri Lanka's largest city and commercial capital, on the west coast.
The official capital is neighbouring Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, where parliament moved in 1982.
A trading port used by Arabs, Portuguese, Dutch and British; capital of British Ceylon from 1815.
Its port is one of the busiest in South Asia.
Q68744: Port city in Fujian on the Taiwan Strait, historically known as Amoy.
One of the treaty ports opened after the First Opium War; Gulangyu islet, with colonial villas, is a World Heritage Site.
One of China's first four Special Economic Zones (1980).
The Taiwanese-held Kinmen islands lie only a few kilometres offshore.
Q16959: Capital of Xinjiang in China's far northwest, at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains.
Often called the city farthest from any ocean in the world (about 2,500 km).
An old stop on the northern Silk Road; home to Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Kazakhs and others.
Was called Dihua until 1954; the name means 'beautiful pasture' in Mongolian.
Q3808: Capital of Cameroon, on seven hills in the centre of the country.
Founded in 1887 by German traders as a base for rubber and ivory.
Became capital of French Cameroon in 1922; Douala remains the larger economic city.
Known for the Reunification Monument and the Mvog-Betsi zoo.
Q1800: Port city on Kerala's Malabar Coast, formerly Cochin; called the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'.
A spice-trade port since the 14th century; Vasco da Gama died and was first buried here in 1524.
Fort Kochi shows Portuguese, Dutch and British influence and its iconic Chinese fishing nets.
Home to an old Jewish community at Mattancherry and India's first fully solar-powered airport.
Q42780: Port city in Zhejiang on the East China Sea, south of Shanghai across Hangzhou Bay.
The port of Ningbo-Zhoushan is the world's busiest port by cargo tonnage.
One of the treaty ports opened after the First Opium War.
Its Tianyi Pavilion (1561) is the oldest surviving private library in China.
Q5465: South Africa's oldest city and seat of its parliament (the 'legislative capital').
Founded in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a supply station for ships to Asia.
Below flat-topped Table Mountain; Cape Point and the Cape of Good Hope are nearby.
Nelson Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island in Table Bay for 18 years.
Q47916: Capital of Uttar Pradesh, on the Gomti River.
Capital of the Nawabs of Awadh in the 18th–19th centuries: the Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza date from then.
Known for its Urdu poetry, courtly etiquette ('tehzeeb'), chikan embroidery and kebabs.
The 1857 Siege of Lucknow was a key event of the Indian Rebellion.
Q374365: Saudi Arabia's second city and main port on the Red Sea.
The gateway for pilgrims to Mecca (65 km east) since Caliph Uthman made it Mecca's port in 647.
Its old town Al-Balad, with coral-stone houses, is a World Heritage Site.
Home of the King Fahd's Fountain, one of the tallest fountains in the world, and the Jeddah Formula 1 circuit.
Q2844: Capital of Brazil since 1960, built from scratch on the central highlands to develop the interior.
Planned by Lúcio Costa with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer; seen from above, the plan looks like an airplane or bird.
Its modernist core is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Founded by President Juscelino Kubitschek, replacing Rio de Janeiro.
Q92161: Capital of Jilin province in Northeast China; the name means 'long spring'.
As Hsinking ('new capital') it was the capital of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo (1932–1945).
Puyi, the last emperor of China, lived in its Imperial Palace of Manchukuo.
China's 'automobile city': home of FAW, the first Chinese carmaker, and a film studio.
Q3894: Capital of Uganda, near the northern shore of Lake Victoria.
Originally built on seven hills; seat of the Buganda kingdom, whose kabaka (king) still has a palace there.
The name comes from 'hill of the impala' in Luganda.
Known for boda-boda motorcycle taxis and the Kasubi Tombs, a World Heritage Site.
Q185684: Capital of Anhui province, north of Chao Lake.
Grew from a small town to a big city after becoming provincial capital in 1952.
A science centre: home of the University of Science and Technology of China and an experimental fusion reactor.
Known as the hometown of Bao Zheng, the famously honest Song-dynasty judge.
Q1362: Capital of Pakistan, a planned city built in the 1960s below the Margalla Hills.
Replaced Karachi as the capital in 1967; designed by Greek planner Constantinos Doxiadis in sectors.
Forms a twin-city metro area with the older Rawalpindi, home of the army headquarters.
Landmark: the Faisal Mosque, shaped like a desert tent.
Q182984: Capital of Kano State and Nigeria's second-largest city, in the dry north.
Over 1,000 years old: one of the seven Hausa city-states and a hub of trans-Saharan trade.
Its old city has mud walls and the Kurmi Market; the Kofar Mata dye pits have been used for centuries.
Seat of the Emir of Kano; mainly Hausa and Muslim.
Q16556: Capital of Arizona, in the Sonoran Desert; the most populous US state capital.
Founded in 1867 on the ruins of ancient Hohokam irrigation canals, so named after the mythical bird rising from ashes.
One of the hottest big cities in the USA, often above 40 °C in summer.
Its 'Valley of the Sun' metro area includes Mesa, Scottsdale and Tempe.
Q34820: Capital of the Dominican Republic, on the south coast of Hispaniola.
Founded in 1496 by Bartholomew Columbus: the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
Its Colonial Zone has the first cathedral, university and fortress of the New World (World Heritage Site).
Was called Ciudad Trujillo under the dictator Trujillo (1936–1961).
Q33935: Israel's economic and tech centre, on the Mediterranean; officially Tel Aviv-Jaffa.
Founded in 1909 as a Jewish suburb of the ancient port of Jaffa; the name means 'hill of spring'.
Its 'White City' of thousands of Bauhaus buildings is a World Heritage Site.
Israel's independence was declared here in 1948; most foreign embassies are here.
Q244898: The most populous city of Taiwan, completely surrounding the capital Taipei.
Called Taipei County until it became a special municipality in 2010.
Includes the old port of Tamsui with the Spanish-built Fort San Domingo, and the mountain town of Jiufen.
Mostly a commuter city for Taipei; seat at Banqiao.
Q192271: Capital of Guizhou province, at about 1,100 m on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau.
Its name means 'precious sun' — locals say sunny days are rare.
Has become China's 'big data' hub, with data centres of Apple, Tencent and Huawei in its cool mountains.
Nearby are the Huangguoshu Waterfall and many ethnic Miao and Buyi villages.
Q35997: Turkey's third city, on the Aegean coast; known in antiquity as Smyrna.
Over 3,000 years old; possibly the birthplace of Homer; ancient Ephesus is about 70 km south.
Largely burned in 1922 at the end of the Greco-Turkish war.
Considered Turkey's most liberal big city; a major port and trade-fair centre.
Q57970: City in southern Jiangsu on the Grand Canal, between Nanjing and Shanghai.
Over 2,500 years old; the Tianning Temple pagoda is one of the tallest in the world.
Birthplace of Zhou Youguang, creator of the pinyin romanization system.
Known for its dinosaur theme park and manufacturing.
Q81788: City on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, part of Greater Cairo.
Home of the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the only surviving one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the Great Sphinx.
The Grand Egyptian Museum, the world's largest archaeological museum, opened near the pyramids.
Ancient Memphis, Egypt's first capital, lies a little to the south.
Q7903: Morocco's largest city and economic centre, on the Atlantic coast.
The Hassan II Mosque has one of the tallest minarets in the world (210 m), partly built over the sea.
Developed by the French as the main port of their protectorate from 1912; known for Art Deco buildings.
Gave its name to the 1942 film 'Casablanca'; hosted the 1943 Allied conference.
Q59223: City in the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong, between Guangzhou and Macau.
Named in 1925 after Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan), founding father of the Republic of China, who was born here.
His former residence in Cuiheng village is a museum.
A manufacturing centre for lighting, furniture and appliances.
Q66485: Capital of Rajasthan, called the 'Pink City' for its pink-painted old town.
Founded in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II as one of India's first planned cities; a World Heritage Site.
Landmarks: Hawa Mahal ('Palace of Winds'), City Palace, Jantar Mantar observatory and nearby Amber Fort.
Part of the 'Golden Triangle' tourist route with Delhi and Agra.
Q2449: Capital of Somalia, on the Indian Ocean; locally called Xamar.
A medieval trading sultanate that controlled the Indian Ocean gold trade; visited by Ibn Battuta.
Capital of Italian Somaliland; devastated by civil war from 1991, including the 1993 'Black Hawk Down' battle.
Q42651: City in southern Jiangsu on the shore of Lake Tai, along the Grand Canal.
A cradle of Chinese national industry and silk production in the early 20th century.
Home of the 88 m Grand Buddha at Ling Shan.
Its Xihui Park and the Jichang Garden are classic sights.
Q100: Capital of Massachusetts and the largest city in New England, on Massachusetts Bay.
Founded in 1630 by English Puritans; the Boston Tea Party (1773) helped start the American Revolution.
Harvard and MIT are in neighbouring Cambridge; a world centre of education and medicine.
Its Boston Marathon is the oldest annual marathon in the world.
Q340: Quebec's largest city, on an island in the St. Lawrence River; named after Mount Royal.
Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie; the second-largest mainly French-speaking city in the world after Paris.
Hosted Expo 67 and the 1976 Summer Olympics.
Known for its Old Town, festivals, bagels and smoked meat.
Q220: Capital of Italy on the Tiber River; called the 'Eternal City'.
According to legend founded by Romulus in 753 BC; centre of the Roman Republic and Empire.
Vatican City, the smallest country in the world and seat of the Pope, lies inside Rome.
Landmarks: the Colosseum, Pantheon, Roman Forum, Trevi Fountain and St. Peter's Basilica.
Q132830: Cameroon's largest city and economic capital, on the estuary of the Wouri River.
Its port is one of the largest in Central Africa and serves landlocked Chad and the Central African Republic.
Was capital of German Kamerun (as Kamerunstadt) until 1901.
Known for makossa music, which comes from here.
Q48344: Capital of Pernambuco in northeast Brazil, built on islands and rivers; called the 'Brazilian Venice'.
Grew as a sugar port; capital of Dutch Brazil (as Mauritsstad) in the 17th century.
Its name means 'reef', after the reefs along its coast.
Neighbouring Olinda is a World Heritage Site; both are famous for frevo and their carnival.
Q956893: Town in northern Kerala, centre of a large urban agglomeration of towns and villages.
Headquarters of Malappuram district, the most populous district in Kerala.
Has close ties with the Gulf states through migrant workers.
Associated with the 1921 Malabar Rebellion against British rule.
Q66568: Large industrial city in Uttar Pradesh on the Ganges; formerly called Cawnpore.
Site of the 1857 Siege of Cawnpore and massacre during the Indian Rebellion.
Once called the 'Manchester of the East' for its textile mills; also known for leather goods.
Home of IIT Kanpur, a leading engineering institute.
Q72778: Capital of Shanxi province, on the Fen River.
Over 2,500 years old and capital of several dynasties; nicknamed the 'Dragon City'.
A centre of coal mining, steel and heavy industry.
The Jinci Temple complex with its Song-dynasty halls is just outside the city.
Q182059: Ghana's second-largest city, capital of the Ashanti Region.
Capital of the Asante Empire, which controlled much of present-day Ghana; the Asantehene (king) still lives here.
Known for the Golden Stool, kente cloth weaving and Kejetia Market, one of the largest markets in West Africa.
Nicknamed the 'Garden City' of West Africa.
Q3766: Capital of Syria; often called the oldest continuously inhabited capital in the world.
Capital of the Umayyad Caliphate; the Umayyad Mosque dates from 715.
Its old city, with the Street Called Straight and covered souqs like Al-Hamidiyah, is a World Heritage Site.
Damascus steel and the damask fabric are named after the city.
Q43463: Capital of Ceará in northeast Brazil, on the Atlantic coast; the name means 'fortress'.
Grew from a Dutch fort built in 1649.
Known for its beaches, kite-surfing nearby and lively nightlife ('forró' music).
Brazil's closest big port to Europe.
Q40269: Capital of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil's southernmost state capital, on Lake Guaíba.
Founded in the 18th century by settlers from the Azores; later many German and Italian immigrants arrived.
Known for the gaúcho culture of the pampas, churrasco and chimarrão (mate).
Hosted the first World Social Forum in 2001.
Q35178: Capital of Kuwait, on Kuwait Bay at the northern end of the Persian Gulf.
Grew from a pearl-diving and trading port into an oil-rich city since the 1950s.
Occupied by Iraq in 1990, which triggered the Gulf War.
Q326891: The East Rand metropolitan municipality in Gauteng, east of Johannesburg; the name means 'place of peace'.
Formed in 2000 from nine towns, including Germiston, Benoni, Boksburg and Kempton Park, which grew with gold mining.
Home of OR Tambo International Airport, Africa's busiest airport.
Q5972: Capital of North Sumatra and Indonesia's largest city outside Java.
Grew in the late 19th century with Dutch tobacco plantations ('Deli tobacco').
Very diverse: Malay, Batak, Chinese, Javanese and Indian communities; the Maimun Palace was the sultan's residence.
Gateway to Lake Toba, the world's largest volcanic lake.
Q3703: Capital of Mali, on the Niger River.
The name means 'crocodile river' in Bambara; the crocodile is the city's symbol.
Grew from a small town into a French colonial capital (1908) and is now one of Africa's fastest-growing cities.
Known for its music scene (e.g. Salif Keïta, Amadou & Mariam).
Q3915: Capital of Madagascar, at about 1,280 m in the central highlands; often shortened to 'Tana'.
Founded around 1610 as a hilltop fortress; capital of the Merina Kingdom.
The Rova, the royal palace complex, sits on the highest hill above the city.
The name means 'city of the thousand' (warriors).
Q3787: Capital of Nigeria since 1991, a planned city in the centre of the country.
Chosen as a neutral site between the Muslim north and the Christian south, replacing Lagos.
Aso Rock, a 400 m granite monolith, overlooks the Presidential Complex; Zuma Rock is just north.
Landmarks: the National Mosque and the National Christian Centre.
Q130514: City on the Nile in Upper Egypt, on the site of ancient Thebes, capital of the New Kingdom.
The Karnak and Luxor temples are in the city; the Valley of the Kings, with Tutankhamun's tomb, is across the river.
Often called the world's greatest open-air museum.
Known for hot-air balloon rides over the West Bank.
Q48278: Colombia's second city, in the Aburrá Valley of the Andes; nicknamed the 'City of Eternal Spring'.
Was the base of Pablo Escobar's drug cartel and one of the world's most violent cities in the early 1990s.
Transformed by urban innovations such as the Metrocable gondolas and outdoor escalators in Comuna 13.
Known for its flower festival and the sculptures of Fernando Botero.
Q42635: Coastal city in southern Zhejiang at the mouth of the Ou River.
Famous for entrepreneurship: Wenzhou merchants built family businesses across China and Europe.
Its 'Wenzhou model' of private enterprise was a pioneer of China's market reforms.
Known for shoe and lighter manufacturing and for the Yandang Mountains nearby.
Q183298: Capital of Oyo State; Nigeria's largest city by area.
In 1960 it was the largest city in Nigeria and second in Africa after Cairo.
Founded in the 19th century as a Yoruba war camp, it became the Ibadan Republic.
Home of the University of Ibadan (1948), Nigeria's oldest university, and Cocoa House, once the tallest building in Africa.
Q171943: Capital of Jiangxi province, near Poyang Lake, China's largest freshwater lake.
The Communist Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 is celebrated as the birth of the People's Liberation Army.
The Tengwang Pavilion is one of the 'Three Great Towers' of southern China.
A key railway hub between eastern and southern China.
Q68481: Capital of Fujian, on the Min River estuary.
Called the 'Banyan City' for its many banyan trees.
One of the treaty ports opened after the First Opium War; its Three Lanes and Seven Alleys district is well preserved.
Origin of many overseas Chinese emigrants; known for Fuzhou fish balls and lacquerware.
Q36947: Capital of Bahia, founded in 1549 as the first capital of colonial Brazil (until 1763).
The centre of Afro-Brazilian culture, shaped by the slave trade: capoeira, candomblé and Bahian cuisine.
Its colourful Pelourinho historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
Has one of the biggest street carnivals in the world.
Q58422: Industrial city in Hebei on the Bohai Sea coast.
Called the 'cradle of Chinese industry': China's first standard-gauge railway and first cement factory were built here.
Almost completely destroyed by the 1976 Tangshan earthquake, which killed about 240,000 people.
A major steel producer and porcelain centre today.
Q2471: Capital of Yemen, at about 2,300 m in the highlands.
Claims to be one of the oldest inhabited cities in the world.
Its Old City, with multi-storey rammed-earth tower houses decorated with white gypsum, is a World Heritage Site.
Controlled by the Houthi movement since 2014, during the civil war.
Q1346536: County-level city in eastern Guangdong, part of the Chaoshan region under Jieyang.
The county-level city with the largest registered population in China.
Known for its textile and clothing trade and for growing green plums and tea.
Part of the Teochew-speaking cultural area.
Q269: Capital of Uzbekistan and the largest city of Central Asia.
An old Silk Road city whose name means 'stone city'.
Conquered by Russia in 1865; largely rebuilt in Soviet style after a big earthquake in 1966.
Its metro stations are famous for their decoration; the Khast Imam complex holds an early Quran manuscript.
Q10392: City east of Jakarta in West Java, one of the largest commuter cities of the Jakarta metropolitan area.
Has a very old history: it was a centre of the 5th-century Tarumanagara kingdom.
A big industrial area with many factories along the Jakarta–Cikampek corridor.
Part of the Jabodetabek megacity, with Bogor, Depok and Tangerang.
Q4361: Capital of Paraná in southern Brazil, on a plateau at about 930 m.
Famous for urban planning: it invented the bus rapid transit (BRT) system with 'tube' stations.
Known for its many parks and the Wire Opera House.
Settled by many European immigrants (Polish, Ukrainian, German, Italian).
